title: My parents will give me RM700,000. Can I buy a RM1.35m condo?
excerpt: A 30-year-old earning RM7,500 has RM700,000 to RM800,000 from his parents for a RM1.35 million tenanted condo. Sean says the gift doesn't change what he can afford.

question.asker: From BK, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: BK is 30, single, earns RM7,500 a month gross, has RM150,000 in savings and a fully paid car. His parents will give him RM700,000 to RM800,000. He has viewed one 2010 subsale condo in Ara Damansara three times, negotiated from RM1.5 million to RM1.35 million, tenanted at RM4,400 a month. He plans a 20-year semi-flexi loan at about RM4,000 a month and to move in after marrying.
question.text: With his parents' money and the rent, is this a sensible first property, and should he put in a bigger down payment or keep the cash in a flexi loan?

answer.quote: It's beyond your affordability, even after an injection of fund from the parents.
answer.summary: No. On his own income he can comfortably carry a property of about RM500,000, and the gift only makes a RM1.35 million unit look affordable. He should buy his first property as an investment without his parents' money, and ask them to hold on to it for now.

reasons.title: His income carries about RM500,000
reasons.body: Net income of about RM6,600 divided by three gives a comfortable instalment of about RM2,200, which suits a property of around RM500,000. To qualify for a RM4,000 instalment on his own he would need to earn about RM12,000 to RM15,000.

reasons.title: The rent only works because the down payment is huge
reasons.body: At a 90% loan of about RM1.21 million the instalment would be about RM5,460, plus maintenance. RM4,400 a month is a yield of only 3.9%, against 5% to 6% for most KL and Klang Valley property, so he would have to put in about 37% just to break even.

reasons.title: Never knock off the principal
reasons.body: Rather than paying down the loan as his parents suggest, park spare cash in a flexi account to cut interest while keeping it available in an emergency. A 20-year tenure also makes little sense when a housing loan is the cheapest money there is.

reasons.title: He skipped the viewing step
reasons.body: Of Sean's four basic steps, his intent is clear but he has only seen this one unit. At RM1.35 million there are many options, new and old, high-rise and landed, so viewing the same unit three times locks him in too early.

actions: Work out what you would buy without the family money, using your own income and savings.
Ask your parents to hold the gift for now, and tell them you will ask when you need it.
Look for a first property across the four buying channels whose rent covers the instalment and maintenance with a surplus.
Learn to invest your own savings, for example in money market funds and stocks, before receiving the larger sum.
When you do buy a home to live in, consider an intermediate terrace with a loan of about RM500,000, which costs roughly RM2,500 to RM2,800 a month.
caveat: The price itself is fair: Brickz data shows a median of about RM760 per sq ft for the development. Sean's objection is affordability, not value, and he would accept a family gift gracefully as long as it comes with no conditions about where to live.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #324. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in the episode; check current loan rates and foreign-buyer price thresholds for your own situation.
